lessons.culture: Wudu is the washing done before prayer: the hands, mouth and nose, face, arms up to the elbows, wiping the head, then the feet. Mosques keep a wudu area, usually near the toilets, shoes come off at the door, and clothes should be clean and modest. People put their phones on silent so no one's prayer is disturbed, and the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah, is often shown by a niche called the mihrab.

lessons.culture: Jumu'ah replaces the Dhuhr prayer on Friday and is prayed in congregation after a khutbah. Many people bathe, put on clean clothes and come early, and during the khutbah everyone listens in silence. In a crowded mosque the rows are filled by moving closer together, and after the prayer people greet each other with جُمُعَةٌ مُبَارَكَة. The fixed wishes (تَقَبَّلَ اللَّه and جَزَاكَ اللَّهُ خَيْرًا) are classical and the same in every dialect; the talk around them is Damascene.

challenge.title: A visit to the masjid
challenge.instructions: Write and act out a short conversation of at least 10 lines in Damascene. Ask about the next prayer and the iqamah, find the wudu area and the qibla, put your shoes on the rack, put your phone on silent, and say what you do when you are late. Keep the fixed Islamic wording classical and put the everyday talk around it in Damascene.
required_elements: a question about the next prayer or the time of the iqamah using شو or إيمتى
a question about the wudu area or the entrance using وين
a request about the shoe rack, the prayer rug or the qibla
a polite request or reply about the phone using لو سمحت or حاضر
a missed rak'ah explained with فاتتني and a closing تَقَبَّلَ اللَّه with its reply مِنَّا وَمِنْكُم
